Alvin Ailey was an American modern dancer and choreographer who founded the Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, the most racially integrated and economically successful dance company in the world. Born in nineteen thirty-one in Texas to a Black mother and white father, he grew up in a segregated South before studying dance in Los Angeles. He studied with Martha Graham, Lester Horton, and others, absorbing a wide range of contemporary and vernacular movement vocabularies. In nineteen fifty-eight, he founded the Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, which became the largest and most acclaimed modern dance company in the world, breaking barriers of race and class in concert dance. He created Revelations in nineteen sixty, set to African-American spirituals, which became the company's signature work and one of the most performed pieces of modern dance. He pioneered the practice of presenting works by other choreographers—including Balanchine, Graham, Cunningham, and Fosse—within a single company, creating a living library of modern dance. He expanded the company's training and outreach, particularly serving inner-city youth through the Alvin Ailey School, making dance accessible across economic barriers. His philosophy of dance for all people fundamentally changed the demographics and mission of concert dance in America.
